## <span class="num">17.3.1</span> Matrix Lie Groups

The finite groups studied so far (symmetric groups, dihedral groups, and so on) are discrete. Many important groups in mathematics and physics are continuous: the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, the group $\GL_n(\RR)$ of invertible matrices, and others. Lie theory studies such groups through linear algebra. We give $\CC^{n \times n} \cong \CC^{n^2}$ its usual topology, in which $A_m \to A$ when every entry converges.

:::definition{17.3.1} Matrix Lie group
A ***matrix Lie group*** is a subgroup $G \subseteq \GL_n(\CC)$ that is closed in $\GL_n(\CC)$: if $A_m \in G$ and $A_m \to A \in \GL_n(\CC)$, then $A \in G$.
:::

A theorem of von Neumann and Cartan, which we do not prove, says that a matrix Lie group is a smooth submanifold of $\CC^{n \times n}$ on which multiplication and inversion are smooth maps; that is, it is a ***Lie group***.

:::example{17.3.2} The classical matrix Lie groups
Each of the following is closed in $\GL_n(\CC)$, being defined by equations in the matrix entries and their complex conjugates (see also Chapter 9).

- $\GL_n(\RR)$ and $\GL_n(\CC)$, the general linear groups.
- $\SL_n(\RR) = \{A \in \GL_n(\RR) : \det A = 1\}$ and $\SL_n(\CC)$, the special linear groups.
- $\mathrm{O}(n) = \{A \in \GL_n(\RR) : A^t A = I\}$, the orthogonal group, and $\mathrm{SO}(n) = \mathrm{O}(n) \cap \SL_n(\RR)$, the group of rotations.
- $\mathrm{U}(n) = \{A \in \GL_n(\CC) : A^* A = I\}$, the unitary group, and $\mathrm{SU}(n) = \mathrm{U}(n) \cap \SL_n(\CC)$.
- $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, \RR) = \{A \in \GL_{2n}(\RR) : A^t J A = J\}$, where $J = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & I_n \\ -I_n & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$, the symplectic group (Section [9.7](/notes/math-55a/9-7-symplectic-forms)).
:::

:::note
The dimension of a Lie group as a manifold can be guessed by counting equations: $\GL_n(\RR)$ has dimension $n^2$; the single equation $\det A = 1$ gives $\dim \SL_n(\RR) = n^2 - 1$; and $A^t A = I$ consists of $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ equations, since $A^tA$ is symmetric, giving $\dim \mathrm{O}(n) = n^2 - \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. The Lie algebras below confirm these counts.
:::

## <span class="num">17.3.2</span> The Matrix Exponential

:::definition{17.3.3} Matrix exponential
For $X \in \CC^{n \times n}$, the ***matrix exponential*** is $$e^X = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{X^k}{k!} = I + X + \frac{X^2}{2!} + \frac{X^3}{3!} + \cdots.$$
:::

The series converges absolutely for every $X$: for the operator norm $\|X\| = \max\{|Xv| : v \in \CC^n,\ |v| = 1\}$, where $|v|$ is the standard length on $\CC^n$, we have $\|XY\| \leq \|X\|\,\|Y\|$, hence $\|X^k\| \leq \|X\|^k$, so the norms of the terms are bounded by those of the series for $e^{\|X\|}$.

:::proposition{17.3.4} Properties of the matrix exponential
Let $X, Y \in \CC^{n \times n}$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $e^0 = I$.
2. If $XY = YX$, then $e^{X+Y} = e^X e^Y$. In particular $e^X$ is invertible with inverse $e^{-X}$, and $t \mapsto e^{tX}$ is a homomorphism $(\RR, +) \to \GL_n(\CC)$.
3. $e^{AXA^{-1}} = A e^X A^{-1}$ for $A \in \GL_n(\CC)$.
4. $\det(e^X) = e^{\Tr X}$.
5. $\frac{d}{dt} e^{tX} = Xe^{tX}$; in particular $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} e^{tX} = X$.
:::

:::proof Proof (sketch)
(i) is clear. For (ii), multiply the two absolutely convergent series and use the binomial theorem, which holds for commuting matrices. For (iii), conjugate the series term by term. For (iv), by (iii) and Theorem [7.5.2](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-2) we may assume $X$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$; then $e^X$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $e^{\lambda_1}, \ldots, e^{\lambda_n}$, so $\det e^X = e^{\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n} = e^{\Tr X}$. For (v), differentiate the series term by term.
:::

## <span class="num">17.3.3</span> Lie Algebras

A Lie group is a curved object, but its tangent space at the identity is a vector space that retains much of the structure of the group. The extra structure it carries is a Lie bracket.

:::definition{17.3.5} Lie algebra
A ***Lie algebra*** over a field $k$ is a $k$-vector space $\mathfrak{g}$ with a bilinear map $[\cdot, \cdot] : \mathfrak{g} \times \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}$, the ***Lie bracket***, such that:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $[X, X] = 0$ for all $X \in \mathfrak{g}$;
2. the ***Jacobi identity*** $[X, [Y, Z]] + [Y, [Z, X]] + [Z, [X, Y]] = 0$ holds for all $X, Y, Z \in \mathfrak{g}$.
:::

Expanding $[X + Y, X + Y] = 0$ shows that (i) implies $[X, Y] = -[Y, X]$; when $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, the two conditions are equivalent.

:::note
On any associative algebra, such as $k^{n \times n}$ or $\End(V)$, the commutator $[X, Y] = XY - YX$ is a Lie bracket: $[X, X] = 0$ is clear, and the Jacobi identity follows by expanding the triple brackets, all twelve terms cancelling in pairs. With this bracket, $k^{n \times n}$ is the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_n(k)$, and $\End(V)$ is $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$.
:::

:::definition{17.3.6} Lie algebra of a matrix Lie group
For a matrix Lie group $G \subseteq \GL_n(\CC)$, the ***Lie algebra*** of $G$ is $$\mathfrak{g} = \operatorname{Lie}(G) = \{X \in \CC^{n \times n} : e^{tX} \in G \text{ for all } t \in \RR\}.$$
:::

We state without proof that $\mathfrak{g}$ is a real vector subspace of $\CC^{n \times n}$ closed under the commutator bracket, so that it is a real Lie algebra, and that it is the tangent space $T_I G$ of $G$ at the identity. By Proposition [17.3.4](/notes/math-55a/17-3-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras#proposition-17-3-4)(v), each $X \in \mathfrak{g}$ is the velocity at $t = 0$ of the curve $t \mapsto e^{tX}$ in $G$.

:::example{17.3.7} Classical Lie algebras
- $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\RR) = \RR^{n \times n}$, of dimension $n^2$.
- $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\RR) = \{X \in \RR^{n \times n} : \Tr X = 0\}$, of dimension $n^2 - 1$: by Proposition [17.3.4](/notes/math-55a/17-3-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras#proposition-17-3-4)(iv), $\det e^{tX} = e^{t \Tr X}$ equals 1 for all $t$ exactly when $\Tr X = 0$.
- $\mathfrak{so}(n) = \{X \in \RR^{n \times n} : X^t = -X\}$, the skew-symmetric matrices, of dimension $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$; differentiating $(e^{tX})^t e^{tX} = I$ at $t = 0$ gives $X^t + X = 0$.
- $\mathfrak{su}(n) = \{X \in \CC^{n \times n} : X^* = -X, \ \Tr X = 0\}$, the traceless skew-Hermitian matrices, of real dimension $n^2 - 1$.
- $\mathfrak{sp}(2n, \RR) = \{X \in \RR^{2n \times 2n} : X^t J + JX = 0\}$, of dimension $n(2n + 1)$: the condition says that $JX$ is symmetric, and $X \mapsto JX$ is a bijection.
:::

The ***exponential map*** of $G$ is $\exp : \mathfrak{g} \to G$, $X \mapsto e^X$.

:::note
Near the identity, the exponential map translates between $G$ and $\mathfrak{g}$. For $X, Y$ near $0$, the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula $$e^X e^Y = e^{X + Y + \frac{1}{2}[X, Y] + \cdots}$$ holds, where the omitted terms are iterated brackets of $X$ and $Y$; so multiplication in $G$ near the identity is determined by the bracket of $\mathfrak{g}$. By the inverse function theorem, $\exp$ is a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of $0 \in \mathfrak{g}$ onto a neighborhood of $I \in G$, since its derivative at $0$ is the identity. It need not be surjective: the matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix} \in \SL_2(\RR)$ is not $e^X$ for any $X \in \mathfrak{sl}_2(\RR)$. For compact connected groups such as $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(n)$, however, $\exp$ is surjective.
:::

## <span class="num">17.3.4</span> Homomorphisms and Representations

:::definition{17.3.8} Lie algebra homomorphism
A linear map $\varphi : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{h}$ between Lie algebras is a ***homomorphism*** if $\varphi([X, Y]) = [\varphi(X), \varphi(Y)]$ for all $X, Y \in \mathfrak{g}$.
:::

We state the next two facts without proof.

:::proposition{17.3.9} The differential of a homomorphism
Let $\Phi : G \to H$ be a continuous homomorphism of matrix Lie groups. There is a unique real-linear map $d\Phi : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{h}$ with $\Phi(e^{tX}) = e^{t\, d\Phi(X)}$ for all $X \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $t \in \RR$, and $d\Phi$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism. Moreover $d(\Psi \circ \Phi) = d\Psi \circ d\Phi$ and $d(\id_G) = \id_{\mathfrak{g}}$, so $G \mapsto \mathfrak{g}$, $\Phi \mapsto d\Phi$ is a functor (Definition [8.2.1](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#definition-8-2-1)) from matrix Lie groups to real Lie algebras.
:::

:::note
Conversely, if $G$ is connected and simply connected (every loop in $G$ can be contracted to a point), every Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{h}$ is $d\Phi$ for a unique $\Phi : G \to H$. Together with Lie’s third theorem (every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a Lie group), this makes the category of simply connected Lie groups equivalent to that of finite-dimensional real Lie algebras. These statements concern Lie groups in general, which need not be matrix groups.
:::

:::definition{17.3.10} Representation of a Lie algebra
A ***representation*** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ on a vector space $V$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism $\rho : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(V)$, that is, a linear map with $\rho([X, Y]) = \rho(X)\rho(Y) - \rho(Y)\rho(X)$.
:::

By Proposition [17.3.9](/notes/math-55a/17-3-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras#proposition-17-3-9), a continuous representation $G \to \GL(V)$ of a matrix Lie group induces a representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ on $V$, its differential.

:::example{17.3.11} The adjoint representation
Every Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ has the ***adjoint representation*** $\ad : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(\mathfrak{g})$, $\ad(X)(Y) = [X, Y]$. It is a homomorphism because of the Jacobi identity: for $Z \in \mathfrak{g}$, $$\begin{aligned}
[\ad X, \ad Y](Z) &= [X, [Y, Z]] - [Y, [X, Z]] \\
&= -[Z, [X, Y]] = [[X, Y], Z] = \ad([X, Y])(Z),
\end{aligned}$$ where the second equality is the Jacobi identity rewritten using antisymmetry.
:::

## <span class="num">17.3.5</span> Structure and Classification

The structure theory of Lie algebras parallels that of finite groups, with ideals in the role of normal subgroups. An ***ideal*** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is a subspace $\mathfrak{i}$ with $[X, Y] \in \mathfrak{i}$ for all $X \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $Y \in \mathfrak{i}$. For subspaces $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b}$, let $[\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b}]$ be the span of the brackets $[X, Y]$ with $X \in \mathfrak{a}$, $Y \in \mathfrak{b}$. A Lie algebra is ***abelian*** if all brackets vanish.

:::definition{17.3.12} Solvable, semisimple, and simple Lie algebras
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra. Its ***derived series*** is $\mathfrak{g}^{(0)} = \mathfrak{g}$, $\mathfrak{g}^{(k+1)} = [\mathfrak{g}^{(k)}, \mathfrak{g}^{(k)}]$.

- $\mathfrak{g}$ is ***solvable*** if $\mathfrak{g}^{(k)} = 0$ for some $k$.
- $\mathfrak{g}$ is ***semisimple*** if its only solvable ideal is $0$.
- $\mathfrak{g}$ is ***simple*** if it is not abelian and its only ideals are $0$ and $\mathfrak{g}$.
:::

:::note
We state the main structure theorems without proof. The sum of two solvable ideals is a solvable ideal, so $\mathfrak{g}$ has a largest solvable ideal $\mathfrak{r}$, its ***radical***, and $\mathfrak{g}$ is semisimple exactly when $\mathfrak{r} = 0$. Over a field of characteristic 0, $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{r} \oplus \mathfrak{s}$ as vector spaces for a semisimple subalgebra $\mathfrak{s}$ (the ***Levi decomposition***), and every semisimple Lie algebra is, uniquely, a direct sum of simple ideals.

The simple Lie algebras over $\CC$ are classified by Dynkin diagrams:

- four infinite families, $A_n = \mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}(\CC)$ ($n \geq 1$), $B_n = \mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\CC)$ ($n \geq 2$), $C_n = \mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\CC)$ ($n \geq 3$), and $D_n = \mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\CC)$ ($n \geq 4$);
- five exceptional algebras, $G_2$, $F_4$, $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$, of dimensions 14, 52, 78, 133, 248.

The classification proceeds through root systems. Given a semisimple $\mathfrak{g}$ and a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}$ (a maximal abelian subalgebra consisting of semisimple elements), the adjoint action of $\mathfrak{h}$ decomposes $\mathfrak{g}$ into root spaces; the resulting set of roots $\Phi \subset \mathfrak{h}^*$ is a root system, which is encoded by its Dynkin diagram. This is one of the great classification theorems of mathematics (Killing, 1888; Cartan, 1894).
:::

:::example{17.3.13} $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\CC)$, the simplest simple Lie algebra
The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\CC)$ of traceless $2 \times 2$ complex matrices has dimension 3, with standard basis $$e = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad f = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad h = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix},$$ satisfying $[h, e] = 2e$, $[h, f] = -2f$, and $[e, f] = h$ (Exercise [17.3](/notes/math-55a/17-3-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras)(1)). It is the Lie algebra of type $A_1$. Its finite-dimensional representations are completely known: for each $n \geq 0$ there is, up to isomorphism, exactly one irreducible representation of dimension $n + 1$, realized on $\Sym^n(\CC^2)$ (Definition [9.10.3](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#definition-9-10-3)). The representation theory of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is the foundation of the general theory.
:::

:::exercise{17.3.14} Exercises
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Verify the relations $[h, e] = 2e$, $[h, f] = -2f$, $[e, f] = h$ for the standard basis of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\CC)$.
2. Show that $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, the real skew-symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices with the commutator bracket, is isomorphic as a Lie algebra to $\RR^3$ with the cross product as bracket.
3. The ***Killing form*** of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is $B(X, Y) = \Tr(\ad X \circ \ad Y)$. Show that for $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{gl}_n(\CC)$, $$B(X, Y) = 2n \Tr(XY) - 2 \Tr X \Tr Y.$$

:::solution
**(1)** Directly: $$\begin{aligned}
[h, e] &= he - eh = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} - \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} = 2e, \\
[h, f] &= hf - fh = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} - \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} = -2f, \\
[e, f] &= ef - fe = \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} - \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix} = h.
\end{aligned}$$

**(2)** A basis of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is $$E_1 = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, \qquad E_2 = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}, \qquad E_3 = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix},$$ and a direct computation gives $[E_1, E_2] = E_3$, $[E_2, E_3] = E_1$, $[E_3, E_1] = E_2$. The standard basis of $\RR^3$ satisfies $e_1 \times e_2 = e_3$, $e_2 \times e_3 = e_1$, $e_3 \times e_1 = e_2$. Let $\varphi : \mathfrak{so}(3) \to \RR^3$ be the linear isomorphism with $\varphi(E_i) = e_i$. Both brackets are bilinear and antisymmetric, so $\varphi([X, Y]) = \varphi(X) \times \varphi(Y)$ holds for all $X, Y$ once it holds for pairs of basis elements, which is what we checked. So $\varphi$ is an isomorphism of Lie algebras.

**(3)** For $A, C \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(\CC)$, the linear map $Z \mapsto AZC$ on $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\CC)$ has trace $\Tr A \cdot \Tr C$: on the basis of matrix units $E_{ij}$, the coefficient of $E_{ij}$ in $AE_{ij}C$ is $A_{ii}C_{jj}$, and $\sum_{i,j} A_{ii}C_{jj} = \Tr A \Tr C$. Now $$\ad X \circ \ad Y(Z) = X(YZ - ZY) - (YZ - ZY)X = XYZ - XZY - YZX + ZYX.$$ The four terms have the form $AZC$ with $(A, C) = (XY, I)$, $(X, Y)$, $(Y, X)$, and $(I, YX)$, so $$B(X, Y) = n\Tr(XY) - \Tr X \Tr Y - \Tr Y \Tr X + n\Tr(YX) = 2n \Tr(XY) - 2 \Tr X \Tr Y.$$ For $X, Y \in \mathfrak{sl}_n(\CC)$, the map $\ad X \circ \ad Y$ preserves $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\CC)$ and kills $I$, and $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\CC) = \mathfrak{sl}_n(\CC) \oplus \CC I$; so the Killing form of $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\CC)$ is $B(X, Y) = 2n\Tr(XY)$. It is nondegenerate: if $X \neq 0$ is traceless, so is $X^*$, and $\Tr(XX^*) = \sum_{i,j} |X_{ij}|^2 > 0$. By Cartan’s criterion, which we do not prove (a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $\CC$ is semisimple if and only if its Killing form is nondegenerate), $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\CC)$ is semisimple.
:::
:::
